title: Hooks and managed settings for people
bridge: Managed settings are like a company-wide ESLint config that every editor loads and nobody can switch off locally. Except Claude Code reads them from a place only an admin controls, the claude.ai admin console or a system file. So no project, user or command-line setting can override them.
intro: A plugin can carry hooks: small scripts that run before or after a tool call on every machine that has the plugin. Managed settings decide which plugins, marketplaces and MCP servers every laptop gets. This lesson writes a safety hook like rhino-core's. Then it writes the managed settings that roll rhino-core out to every engineer, with an MCP allow-list.

picture.caption: One policy, written by Platform, reaches every laptop and agent VM; the plugin it forces on brings its hooks along.

steps.text: merges the G0, G1 and G8 keys into one reviewed policy
loads above user, project and command-line settings; nobody overrides it
the same file and a seeded plugin folder are baked into the image
the rhino marketplace is known and rhino-core is forced on
before every Write or Edit, the hook reads the call and may refuse it
only servers on the allow-list load, claude.ai connectors included

sections.h: Hooks in a plugin run on every machine
p: Lesson p8-4 wrote hooks as TypeScript functions inside Nova's harness. A plugin hook is the same idea for every Claude Code user, written as a command. Claude Code runs the command at the event and sends the event as JSON on its stdin. It reads the answer from the exit code and output.

Exit code 0 lets the call go on. Exit code 2 blocks it, and whatever the script printed on stderr goes back to Claude as the reason. timeout is in seconds. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the plugin's own folder, wherever it was installed.

G8-09 gives rhino-core two hooks. Before a write, refuse content that looks like a secret or an edit to a credential file. After an edit, lint that one file and show the result. The matcher names MultiEdit because G8-09 does. The hooks docs we checked do not list a MultiEdit tool, so check the current tool names before you ship it.
sections.because: We declare hooks in the plugin's hooks.json, so every machine with the plugin runs them with no setup.

notes.text: A description shown in the plugin's details, so a reviewer knows what runs.
PreToolUse runs before the tool. It can refuse the call.
The matcher names the tools: Write, Edit and MultiEdit. Read and Bash calls never start this hook.
A command hook: python3 runs the script from the plugin's folder. 5 seconds at most.
PostToolUse runs after the tool. It cannot undo the edit, but it can tell Claude what is wrong.
The lint hook gets 60 seconds, because a linter on a large file can be slow.

callout.text: The hooks are Python 3, stdlib only, unlike the TypeScript platform. python3 ships with git's Command Line Tools on every Mac, and Node does not. A hook must run on every laptop with no install step.

p: The script reads the event, looks at the file path and the new text, and decides. It looks for AWS access keys, GitHub and Slack tokens, and private key blocks. It also refuses paths like .env*, *.pem, id_rsa* and anything under a secrets/ folder.

Its message is short and says what to do instead. The lint hook, lint_after_edit.py, works the other way round: it never blocks, and it stays silent when the file is clean. It runs biome check for frontend .ts and .tsx files, and black, isort and flake8 for Python under cloud/, client/ and sdk/.
sections.because: We refuse a secret before it is written, because a pasted secret is the most common leak and the cheapest to stop.

code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PreToolUse hook (a lab version of G8-09): refuse secrets and credential files."""
import json
import re
import sys

SECRET = re.compile(r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}|xox[baprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----")
CREDENTIAL_FILE = re.compile(r"(^|/)(\.env[^/]*|[^/]+\.pem|id_rsa[^/]*)$|(^|/)secrets/")

event = json.load(sys.stdin)
args = event.get("tool_input", {})
path = args.get("file_path", "")
text = args.get("content", "") + args.get("new_string", "")
if CREDENTIAL_FILE.search(path):
    print(f"{path} looks like a credential file. Keep secrets out of the repo.", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)
if SECRET.search(text):
    print("This text looks like a secret (a key, token or private key). Use a placeholder.", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(2)
sys.exit(0)

notes.text: A docstring: this is the lab version. The real one also reads MultiEdit's list of edits.
Secret shapes: an AWS key id, GitHub tokens (ghp_ and friends), Slack tokens, PEM private key blocks.
Credential paths: .env files, .pem files, id_rsa keys and any secrets/ folder.
Claude Code sends the event as JSON on stdin; json.load reads it.
tool_input holds the tool's arguments, for example file_path and content for Write.
Write sends content, Edit sends new_string. Checking both covers both tools.
stderr is what Claude reads as the reason, so the message says what to do instead.
Exit 2 blocks the call.
Exit 0: no problem found, the write goes ahead.

sections.h: Why a hook change is high risk
p: A hook, an MCP server or a script in a plugin runs code on every machine that has the plugin. allowed-tools in a skill's frontmatter skips permission prompts. A Snyk audit found critical issues in 13% of public skills, so these changes need a careful look.

G8-08 adds two jobs to plugin CI. secrets runs gitleaks over the PR's commits. risk finds changes to hooks/, bin/, scripts/, monitors/, .mcp.json or allowed-tools lines. It adds a high-risk label and one comment, edited in place on later pushes.

The label informs the one reviewer, who runs the plugin locally before approving. It is not an extra approval. A new MCP server also needs Ronen from Security and an entry in the managed allow-list. So prefer a skill that runs a CLI over a new server.
sections.because: We find risky files with a plain git diff, so anyone can read the rule and it runs in seconds.

code.text:
- name: Find changes that run code or skip prompts on every machine
        id: risk
        run: |
          base="origin/${{ github.base_ref }}"
          git diff --name-only "$base"...HEAD | grep -E '(^|/)(hooks|bin|scripts|monitors)/|\.mcp\.json$' > risky.txt || true
          git diff "$base"...HEAD -- '**/SKILL.md' | grep -E '^[+-](allowed-tools|disallowed-tools):' >> risky.txt || true
          echo "count=$(wc -l < risky.txt | tr -d ' ')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.text: One step with a plain name, so the reviewer sees why the label appeared.
The PR's base branch, for example origin/main.
Changed files under hooks, bin, scripts or monitors, or any .mcp.json, go into risky.txt.
allowed-tools and disallowed-tools lines that changed in any SKILL.md are added too.
The number of risky lines becomes a step output. The next step labels and comments when it is not 0.

p: Your ~/.claude/settings.json is yours: you can edit it, and a project's settings or a --settings flag can change what it says. Managed settings are the policy tier above all of those. No user, project, local or command-line value overrides them.

They reach a machine in one of three ways. Server-managed settings come from the claude.ai admin console, fetched at startup and every hour. An MDM profile, pushed by a device-management tool like Fleet, is the second. A file is the third: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json on a Mac, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json on Linux.

Next to that file, a managed-settings.d/ folder holds drop-ins: *.json files merged in name order. Our source lives in RhinoHealth/ai-agents/settings/managed-settings.d/, with G0's 10-models.json and G1's telemetry file (lessons g0-6 and g1-1). In a session, /status shows a Setting sources line that names the managed source.

callout.text: Sessions that sign in with a Console API key do not receive server-managed settings. That is one reason the agents' VMs get the policy as a file in the image instead.

sections.h: The policy, part 1: marketplaces and plugins
p: G8-16 adds the plugin and MCP keys to the one policy, next to G0's model block and G1's telemetry block. Platform is its single writer, because G0, G1 and G8 all edit it. The sketch has comments for reading; the real file is plain JSON. It is 29 lines, in two blocks with nothing removed.

strictKnownMarketplaces is the list of sources anyone may add a marketplace from. extraKnownMarketplaces adds ours for everyone. enabledPlugins with true forces a plugin on. A forced plugin cannot be swapped per person, so pilots who want rhino-latest need their own profile.
sections.because: We force one tested plugin on for everyone, because asking each person to install it means half of them never do.

notes.text: One policy for G0, G1 and G8 keys. One writer avoids two teams overwriting each other.
Our marketplaces: any repo under RhinoHealth, any ref or path.
Anthropic's official marketplace, where figma and frontend-design come from. A decision for Ronen.
skills-dir keeps people's own ~/.claude/skills loading.
The rhino catalog from lesson p12-1, at the stable branch.
autoUpdate: laptops pick up a new plugin version without anyone running a command.
rhino-core forced on. The guild plugins are enabled per repo, in fcp/.claude/settings.json.

sections.h: The policy, part 2: the MCP allow-list
p: allowManagedMcpServersOnly with allowedMcpServers means only listed MCP servers load. The list also filters the claude.ai connectors Claude Code fetches itself, like Jira, Slack and Figma. So the rollout starts with an inventory: on 5 laptops run claude mcp list and /plugin, and list the connectors people use.

The Rhino MCP server is allowed only on mcp-dev3, which holds test data. Production reaches customer data, and PHI never enters a prompt. deniedModels keeps G0's Fable block, and env holds G1's telemetry settings with prompt and tool content turned off.
sections.because: We allow MCP servers by URL, because a server that reaches customer data must never load on a laptop by accident.

code.text:
"allowManagedMcpServersOnly": true,
  "allowedMcpServers": [
    { "serverUrl": "https://mcp-dev3.example.com/*" },                // Rhino MCP on test data; prod reaches customer data
    { "serverUrl": "https://<compliance connector host>/*" },             // from G6-13 (Nave)
    { "serverUrl": "https://<each connector in the inventory>/*" }        // Jira, Slack, Figma: don't cut what people use
  ],
  "deniedModels": ["fable"],                                              // G0: Fable needs 30-day retention (a compliance call)
  "env": {                                                                // G1 owns this block
    "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY": "1",
    "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT": "https://<otel collector on inf>",
    "OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS": "0",
    "OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS": "0"
  }
}

notes.text: Only servers on the list below may load, from any source.
Rhino MCP on dev3, with test data only. Production is left off on purpose.
The compliance connector from G6-13, once Nave gives its host.
One entry per connector in the inventory, so the policy does not cut what people use.
G0's block: Fable needs 30-day retention, a compliance call nobody made.
G1 owns the env block: telemetry on, sent to the collector on inf.
Content off: prompts and tool details never leave the laptop in telemetry.

callout.text: PHI never enters a prompt. The allow-list is how a laptop is kept from loading an MCP server that reaches production data.

sections.h: Rolling it out to people and agents
p: Decide the delivery with DevOps and Ronen. The claude.ai admin console gives one policy for the whole org and needs the Owner role. Fleet MDM profiles let pilots get a second profile with rhino-latest.

Pilot on 3 people for 2 days. On each laptop, /status must show the managed source and /plugin must list rhino-core. Then turn it on for everyone, and retire the claude.ai org copies of ticket-to-pr and fcp-lab.
Agents get the same thing. The G3 image bakes the stable catalog into a seed folder (CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR) and carries the same policy file. Nova runs exactly what people run.

lab.title: A secret guard hook and a policy check
youNeed: python3 (comes with git's Command Line Tools)

worked.do: cd ~/plugin-lab && mkdir -p plugins/hello/hooks. Save section 2's script as plugins/hello/hooks/guard_write.py.
echo '{"tool_name":"Write","tool_input":{"file_path":"src/config.ts","content":"export const key = \"AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE\";"}}' | python3 plugins/hello/hooks/guard_write.py; echo "exit $?"
worked.see:
This text looks like a secret (a key, token or private key). Use a placeholder.
exit 2

frontend/.env.local looks like a credential file. Keep secrets out of the repo.
exit 2

worked.do: echo '{"tool_name":"Write","tool_input":{"file_path":"src/config.ts","content":"export const region = \"eu-west-1\";"}}' | python3 plugins/hello/hooks/guard_write.py; echo "exit $?"
In a scratch folder: claude --plugin-dir ~/plugin-lab/plugins/hello, then ask: create src/config.ts that exports the AWS key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
worked.see: The Write is refused with the hook's message, and Claude offers a placeholder or an environment variable instead. The wording varies.
added <n> packages in a few seconds

worked.do: Add a careless drop-in: echo '{ "model": "claude-opus-5-5", "allowedMcpServers": [{ "serverName": "notes" }] }' > settings/managed-settings.d/40-oops.json, and run the check again.

lab.faded: The guard also blocks frontend/.env.example, a file that holds no secrets and belongs in git. Change CREDENTIAL_FILE so .env.example passes while .env and .env.local are still refused. Left to you: the new regular expression. Prove it with the echo command from step 3 and a second one for .env.example.
lab.alone: Write a PostToolUse hook, plugins/hello/hooks/check_json.py, for the lint idea. When the edited file ends in .json, it parses the file with json.load. On an error it prints {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PostToolUse", "additionalContext": "<the error>"}} on stdout and exits 0, so it never blocks. Test it by piping a fake event that points at a broken JSON file.
lab.done: The guard exits 2 for the key and the .env.local edit, and 0 for the harmless write. The plugin validates, and the policy check fails only after the careless drop-in.

quiz.q: A person puts "enabledPlugins": { "rhino-core@rhino": false } in their ~/.claude/settings.json. Managed settings force it to true. What happens?

options.text: rhino-core stays on: managed settings sit above user settings, and nobody overrides them
options.why: That is the point of the policy tier.

options.text: rhino-core turns off, because the user's choice wins on their own laptop
options.why: User settings rank below managed settings.

options.text: Claude Code refuses to start until the conflict is fixed
options.why: There is no conflict to fix; the higher tier wins.

quiz.q: A hook script prints a reason on stderr and exits with code 2. What does Claude Code do?

options.text: It ignores the output and lets the call go on
options.why: Exit 0 lets it go on. Exit 2 blocks.

options.text: It crashes the session with the hook's message
options.why: A hook never crashes the session; it decides one tool call.

options.text: It blocks the tool call and gives the stderr text to Claude as the reason
options.why: So the message should say what to do instead.

quiz.q: Why does G8-16 start with an inventory of MCP servers and connectors on 5 laptops?

options.text: Because Claude Code needs the inventory to download the servers
options.why: The inventory is for people; Claude Code does not read it.

options.text: Because allowedMcpServers also filters claude.ai connectors, so a missing entry would cut tools people use every day
options.why: Jira, Slack and Figma connectors need entries too.

options.text: Because each laptop needs its own allow-list
options.why: One policy applies to everyone; the inventory feeds that one list.

words.plain: A plugin hook that runs a command: the event arrives as JSON on stdin, and exit 2 blocks the call.
The installed plugin's own folder, used in hooks.json to find the plugin's scripts.
The policy tier of Claude Code settings, set by an admin; no user, project or flag can override it.
Managed settings pushed from the claude.ai admin console, fetched at startup and every hour.
One *.json file in managed-settings.d/; the files are merged in name order.
allowedMcpServers with allowManagedMcpServersOnly: only listed servers and connectors may load.
The label plugin CI puts on PRs that change hooks, scripts, MCP config or allowed-tools.

tickets.why: rhino-core's two hooks: refuse secrets and credential files before a write, lint the file after an edit.
Plugin CI flags hook, script and MCP changes as high risk, because they run on every machine.
The managed-settings rollout: our marketplaces only, rhino-core forced on, an MCP allow-list, a pilot first.
The first managed-settings keys (Fable denied, agent teams off) that G8-16's policy keeps.

remember: Plugin hooks run on every machine with the plugin, and managed settings decide, above everyone, what those machines get.
